body: What problem does HTTPS solve that HTTP does not?

options.body: Confidentiality and integrity of traffic, plus server identity
Faster page loads
options.whyWrong: HTTPS adds a handshake, though HTTP/2 over TLS often ends up faster overall.

options.body: Better compression
options.whyWrong: Compression is negotiated independently of TLS.

options.body: Guaranteed delivery
options.whyWrong: Delivery guarantees come from TCP beneath it.

explanation: TLS encrypts the traffic, detects tampering, and authenticates the server via a certificate chain. Without it, anyone on the path can read and modify the exchange — which is why certificate warnings should never be clicked past.
concept: TLS provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication — three properties, not one.
hint: What can someone on the same Wi-Fi see over plain HTTP?

body: What is the difference between a switch and a hub?

options.body: A switch forwards a frame only to the port with the destination MAC; a hub repeats it everywhere
A hub is faster
options.whyWrong: Repeating to every port wastes bandwidth and causes collisions.

options.body: A switch works only with fibre
options.whyWrong: Both work over copper or fibre.

options.body: A hub operates at layer 3
options.whyWrong: A hub is a layer-1 repeater with no addressing at all.

explanation: A switch learns which MAC lives behind each port and forwards selectively, so several conversations proceed at once. A hub is an electrical repeater, putting every device in one collision domain — which is why hubs disappeared.
concept: Selective forwarding is what lets a switch give each port its own bandwidth.
hint: What happens when two devices transmit at once on a hub?

body: What does a load balancer’s health check accomplish?

options.body: It stops traffic being sent to instances that are failing
It measures CPU usage for billing
options.whyWrong: Billing is unrelated to health checking.

options.body: It encrypts traffic to the backend
options.whyWrong: Encryption is a separate configuration.

options.body: It caches responses
options.whyWrong: Caching is a distinct function.

explanation: The balancer polls each backend and removes failing ones from rotation, so users are not routed to a broken instance. A check that only tests whether the port is open will happily keep sending traffic to a process that has stopped serving correctly.
concept: A health check is only as good as the thing it actually tests.
hint: Is an open port the same as a working service?

body: Why is idempotency important when a client retries a request over an unreliable network?

options.body: The client cannot tell whether a timed-out request was processed, so a repeat must be safe
Retries are always faster than the original
options.whyWrong: Speed is not the concern.

options.body: Idempotent requests skip the network stack
options.whyWrong: Every request goes over the network.

options.body: Non-idempotent requests cannot time out
options.whyWrong: Any request can time out.

explanation: A timeout means the response was lost, which may or may not mean the request was. If the operation is idempotent, retrying is harmless. If not — a payment, say — you need an idempotency key so the server recognises the duplicate.
concept: Design for the case where the client does not know what happened.
hint: What might have happened to a request that timed out?

body: In the edit-distance DP between two strings, what does dp[i][j] hold?

options.body: The minimum edits to turn the first i characters of one string into the first j of the other
Whether the two prefixes are equal
options.whyWrong: A boolean cannot express a minimum cost.

options.body: The length of their longest common subsequence
options.whyWrong: That is a different recurrence with a different meaning.

options.body: The number of differing characters
options.whyWrong: Simple mismatch counting only works for equal-length strings and ignores insertions.

explanation: When the characters match the cost carries over from dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise it is one plus the cheapest of insert, delete or replace. Defining the state over prefix pairs is what makes the recurrence close.
concept: Most two-string DP problems index by a prefix of each string.
hint: What are the two things a subproblem depends on here?

body: The longest palindromic substring DP fills its table in what order, and why?

options.body: By increasing substring length, because a longer substring depends on a shorter inner one
Left to right by starting index
options.whyWrong: A left-to-right sweep can reach a cell before the inner substring it needs is computed.

options.body: In any order, since the cells are independent
options.whyWrong: The cells are not independent — that dependence is what makes it DP.

options.body: From the end backwards by character
options.whyWrong: Character order alone does not respect the dependency.

explanation: dp[i][j] is true when the characters at i and j match and dp[i+1][j−1] is already true. That inner substring is two characters shorter, so filling by increasing length guarantees it is ready when needed.
concept: Fill order must follow the dependency direction of the recurrence.
hint: Which cell must already be computed before dp[i][j] can be?

body: A table stores (student_id, course_id, student_name, course_fee). Which normal form does it violate first?

options.body: Second normal form, because student_name depends on only part of the composite key
First normal form, because a column holds multiple values
options.whyWrong: Every column here holds a single atomic value, so 1NF is satisfied.

options.body: Third normal form, because of a transitive dependency
options.whyWrong: A partial dependency on the composite key breaks 2NF first, before any 3NF question arises.

options.body: Boyce-Codd normal form, because of an overlapping candidate key
options.whyWrong: BCNF violations are considered only once 3NF holds.

explanation: The key is (student_id, course_id). student_name depends on student_id alone and course_fee on course_id alone — both partial dependencies, which is exactly what 2NF forbids.
concept: Partial dependency on part of a composite key = 2NF violation.

body: A relation has key emp_id and columns dept_id and dept_head, where dept_head is determined by dept_id. Which normal form is violated?

options.body: Third normal form, because dept_head depends transitively on the key
Second normal form
options.whyWrong: The key is a single attribute, so no partial dependency is possible and 2NF holds.

options.body: First normal form
options.whyWrong: All values are atomic, so 1NF holds.

options.body: No normal form is violated
options.whyWrong: A non-key attribute determining another non-key attribute is precisely a 3NF violation.

explanation: emp_id determines dept_id, and dept_id determines dept_head, so dept_head depends on the key only transitively. 3NF forbids exactly that.
concept: Non-key attribute determining another non-key attribute = 3NF violation.

body: What does the isolation level READ COMMITTED prevent that READ UNCOMMITTED does not?

options.body: Dirty reads — seeing rows written by a transaction that has not yet committed
Non-repeatable reads
options.whyWrong: READ COMMITTED still allows a row to change between two reads in the same transaction.

options.body: Phantom reads
options.whyWrong: Phantoms are prevented only at SERIALIZABLE (or with range locks).

options.body: Lost updates
options.whyWrong: Lost updates are not addressed by moving from READ UNCOMMITTED to READ COMMITTED.

explanation: READ COMMITTED guarantees every row you read was committed at the moment you read it, eliminating dirty reads. Rows can still change between two reads in the same transaction.
concept: Dirty read → READ COMMITTED. Non-repeatable read → REPEATABLE READ. Phantom → SERIALIZABLE.

body: Two transactions each read a row and then write it back with an increment. Both start from the same value. What anomaly is this?

options.body: A lost update — one increment overwrites the other
A dirty read
options.whyWrong: Neither transaction reads uncommitted data; both read a committed value.

options.body: A phantom read
options.whyWrong: Phantoms concern rows appearing in a repeated range query, not a single row.

options.body: A deadlock
options.whyWrong: Nothing here forces either transaction to wait on the other.

explanation: Both read the same starting value and both write value+1, so the second write silently discards the first increment. The fix is an atomic update, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or optimistic version checking.
concept: Read-modify-write without locking or an atomic UPDATE loses one of the writes.

body: What is the durability guarantee in ACID?

options.body: Once a transaction commits, its effects survive a crash or power loss
A transaction sees a consistent snapshot for its whole duration
options.whyWrong: That describes isolation, not durability.

options.body: All of a transaction's statements succeed or none do
options.whyWrong: That is atomicity.

options.body: The database never violates its declared constraints
options.whyWrong: That is consistency.

explanation: Durability means a committed transaction is on stable storage — typically because the write-ahead log entry was flushed before the commit was acknowledged.
concept: Durability is what the write-ahead log buys you: commit acknowledged means recoverable.

body: A query filters on a low-cardinality column such as gender over a 50-million-row table. Why may an index not help?

options.body: Each value matches a large fraction of the table, so the planner prefers a sequential scan over many random row lookups
Indexes cannot be built on low-cardinality columns
options.whyWrong: They can; the question is whether the planner will use them.

options.body: The index would be larger than the table
options.whyWrong: A single-column index is far smaller than a wide table.

options.body: Low-cardinality columns cannot be compared with equality
options.whyWrong: Equality comparison works regardless of cardinality.

explanation: An index is worthwhile when it eliminates most rows. If a value matches, say, half the table, following the index means millions of random heap lookups — usually slower than reading the table sequentially.
concept: Indexes pay off at low selectivity ratios; a scan wins when a predicate matches a large share of rows.

body: A composite index exists on (last_name, first_name). Which query can use it effectively?

options.body: WHERE last_name = 'Rao' AND first_name = 'Asha'
WHERE first_name = 'Asha'
options.whyWrong: A composite index cannot be seeked on its second column alone; the leading column must be constrained.

options.body: WHERE UPPER(last_name) = 'RAO'
options.whyWrong: Wrapping the column in a function prevents an index seek unless an expression index exists.

options.body: WHERE last_name LIKE '%ao'
options.whyWrong: A leading wildcard makes the prefix unknown, so no range can be located.

explanation: A B-tree composite index is ordered by its leading column first. Queries must constrain that leading column — and must leave it unwrapped by functions — for a seek to be possible.
concept: Leftmost-prefix rule: constrain columns from the left, and never wrap the column in a function.

body: What is the practical difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?

options.body: A clustered index determines the physical order of the rows, so a table can have only one
A clustered index is always faster for every query
options.whyWrong: Clustering helps range scans on the clustering key; it does not help all queries.

options.body: A non-clustered index cannot be unique
options.whyWrong: Non-clustered indexes can certainly enforce uniqueness.

options.body: A clustered index stores only the key, not the row
options.whyWrong: It is the opposite: the clustered index holds the full rows at its leaves.

explanation: The clustered index is the table: its leaf level holds the actual rows in key order. Since rows can be stored in only one order, there is at most one clustered index per table.
concept: Clustered index = the table itself, in key order. Everything else points into it.

body: In an ER diagram, how is a many-to-many relationship between Student and Course implemented relationally?

options.body: With a junction table holding student_id and course_id as a composite key
With a foreign key from Course to Student
options.whyWrong: A single foreign key can only express many-to-one.

options.body: With a foreign key from Student to Course
options.whyWrong: This has the same limitation in the other direction.

options.body: With a repeating course_id column on Student
options.whyWrong: Repeating groups violate first normal form and cap the relationship arbitrarily.

explanation: Relational tables cannot express many-to-many directly. The standard resolution is an associative (junction) table whose primary key is the pair of foreign keys.
concept: Every M:N relationship becomes a third table.

body: What distinguishes a weak entity in an ER model?

options.body: It has no key of its own and is identified only in combination with its owner entity
It has fewer attributes than other entities
options.whyWrong: Attribute count has nothing to do with weakness.

options.body: It participates in no relationships
options.whyWrong: A weak entity necessarily participates in an identifying relationship.

options.body: It can be deleted without affecting other entities
options.whyWrong: The opposite holds: deleting the owner removes the weak entity.

explanation: A weak entity lacks a sufficient key of its own — an OrderLine is identified only as line n of order m — so its primary key includes the owner's key.
concept: Weak entity: partial key + owner key = primary key.

body: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do on a foreign key?

options.body: Deleting the parent row automatically deletes the child rows that reference it
It prevents the parent row from being deleted while children exist
options.whyWrong: That is ON DELETE RESTRICT or NO ACTION.

options.body: It sets the child's foreign key to NULL when the parent is deleted
options.whyWrong: That is ON DELETE SET NULL.

options.body: It deletes the parent when the last child is deleted
options.whyWrong: No referential action works in that direction.

explanation: CASCADE propagates the delete downward from parent to children, keeping referential integrity without an application-level cleanup step.
concept: CASCADE deletes downward; RESTRICT blocks; SET NULL orphans the child.

body: Why does a database use a write-ahead log?

options.body: So a commit can be acknowledged after a small sequential log write, with the data pages flushed later
To keep a readable history of all queries executed
options.whyWrong: The WAL records page changes for recovery, not a query audit trail.

options.body: To compress the data files
options.whyWrong: Compression is unrelated to the WAL's purpose.

options.body: To allow queries to run without acquiring any locks
options.whyWrong: Some engines use the log for MVCC snapshots, but that is not why the WAL exists.

explanation: Writing a small sequential log record is far cheaper than flushing scattered data pages. The log makes the commit durable immediately, and recovery replays it to rebuild any pages lost in a crash.
concept: WAL turns many random writes into one sequential write, and makes crash recovery replayable.

body: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?

options.body: DELETE removes rows one at a time and can be filtered; TRUNCATE removes all rows as a single operation
TRUNCATE can be rolled back but DELETE cannot
options.whyWrong: Both are transactional in most engines; the claim is reversed for those where it differs.

options.body: DELETE removes the table structure as well
options.whyWrong: That is DROP TABLE.

options.body: TRUNCATE accepts a WHERE clause
options.whyWrong: TRUNCATE has no WHERE clause — that is its main limitation.

explanation: DELETE is a normal DML statement: row by row, filterable, and fires row triggers. TRUNCATE deallocates the storage wholesale, which is much faster but all-or-nothing.
concept: DELETE = filtered and per-row. TRUNCATE = whole table, no WHERE.

body: A stored procedure and a view are both used to encapsulate a query. What is the key difference?

options.body: A view is referenced like a table in a query; a procedure is invoked and can contain control flow and multiple statements
A view always stores its results physically
options.whyWrong: Only a materialised view does; an ordinary view is a stored query definition.

options.body: A procedure cannot take parameters
options.whyWrong: Parameters are one of a procedure's main features.

options.body: A view can modify data but a procedure cannot
options.whyWrong: Procedures routinely modify data; views are updatable only in restricted cases.

explanation: A view is a named query you can select from and join against. A procedure is executable code — parameters, branching, loops, several statements — invoked rather than queried.
concept: View = a virtual table. Procedure = a callable routine.

body: What problem does a materialised view solve that a normal view does not?

options.body: It stores the computed result, so an expensive aggregation is not recomputed on every read
It guarantees the result is always current
options.whyWrong: A materialised view is only as fresh as its last refresh — that is its main trade-off.

options.body: It allows joins across databases
options.whyWrong: Cross-database access is unrelated to materialisation.

options.body: It enforces referential integrity
options.whyWrong: Integrity is enforced by constraints, not by views.

explanation: A materialised view trades freshness for speed: the result is persisted and refreshed on a schedule or on demand, so heavy aggregations are paid for once instead of per query.
concept: Materialised view = a cached query result, with staleness as the price.

body: Which situation makes a NoSQL document store a better fit than a relational database?

options.body: Records with varying, evolving shapes that are almost always read whole by their own id
Data requiring multi-row transactions across several entity types
options.whyWrong: That is the classic strength of a relational engine.

options.body: Data queried mainly through ad-hoc joins across many tables
options.whyWrong: Joins are exactly what document stores handle poorly.

options.body: Any dataset larger than a few gigabytes
options.whyWrong: Relational databases handle far larger datasets routinely; size alone decides nothing.

explanation: Document stores suit self-contained aggregates with irregular fields fetched by key. Once your access pattern is ad-hoc joins or cross-entity transactions, a relational engine is usually the better tool.
concept: Choose by access pattern, not by data volume.

body: Which join returns every row from the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match?

options.body: LEFT OUTER JOIN
INNER JOIN
options.whyWrong: An inner join drops left rows that have no match.

options.body: RIGHT OUTER JOIN
options.whyWrong: That preserves the right table instead.

options.body: CROSS JOIN
options.whyWrong: A cross join pairs every left row with every right row and has no match condition.

explanation: A LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves all rows of the left table; unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL.
concept: LEFT JOIN keeps the left side whole. Filtering the right side in WHERE silently turns it back into an inner join.

body: A LEFT JOIN is written and then filtered with "WHERE right_table.status = 'active'". What happens?

options.body: The join behaves as an inner join, because the NULL rows fail the WHERE predicate
Nothing changes; the outer join still preserves all left rows
options.whyWrong: Unmatched rows have NULL in status, and NULL = 'active' is not true, so they are filtered out.

options.body: It raises an error because NULLs cannot be compared
options.whyWrong: Comparing NULL is legal; it simply yields unknown.

options.body: Only rows with status IS NULL are returned
options.whyWrong: The predicate selects 'active', so NULL rows are excluded rather than selected.

explanation: Predicates on the right table belong in the ON clause of an outer join. Placed in WHERE, they run after the join and discard the very NULL-extended rows the outer join produced.
concept: Filter the outer table in ON; filter the preserved table in WHERE.

body: What does a SELF JOIN accomplish?

options.body: It relates rows of a table to other rows of the same table, such as employees to their managers
It duplicates every row in the table
options.whyWrong: That would be a cross join to itself without a predicate — a symptom, not the purpose.

options.body: It joins a table to its own index
options.whyWrong: Indexes are not join operands.

options.body: It joins a table to a copy stored in another schema
options.whyWrong: A self join uses one table with two aliases, not a copy.

explanation: A self join lists the table twice under different aliases so that hierarchical or comparative relationships within one table can be expressed as an ordinary join.
concept: Self join = one table, two aliases, joined on a relationship within the data.

body: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

options.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
HAVING is faster than WHERE
options.whyWrong: Performance is not the distinction; the stage at which they run is.

options.body: WHERE cannot be used with GROUP BY
options.whyWrong: WHERE is used with GROUP BY routinely, to filter the input rows.

options.body: HAVING works only with COUNT
options.whyWrong: HAVING works with any aggregate expression.

explanation: WHERE runs before rows are grouped, so it cannot reference an aggregate. HAVING runs after grouping and is the only place an aggregate can be filtered.
concept: Filter rows in WHERE, filter aggregates in HAVING — put what you can in WHERE, it is cheaper.

body: What does COUNT(column) return for rows where that column is NULL?

options.body: Those rows are not counted; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values only
They are counted as zero values
options.whyWrong: COUNT does not substitute a value for NULL; it skips the row.

options.body: The whole result becomes NULL
options.whyWrong: A NULL input does not poison COUNT.

options.body: It raises an error
options.whyWrong: Counting a nullable column is perfectly legal.

explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts rows where that column is not NULL. The gap between the two is a quick way to count missing values.
concept: COUNT(*) = rows. COUNT(col) = non-NULL values of col.

body: A table has salaries 100, 200, NULL and 300. What does AVG(salary) return?

options.body: 200, because NULL is excluded from both the sum and the count
150, because the NULL counts as zero
options.whyWrong: Aggregates ignore NULL entirely rather than treating it as zero.

options.body: NULL, because one input is NULL
options.whyWrong: Only if every input were NULL would AVG return NULL.

options.body: 600, which is the sum rather than the average
options.whyWrong: AVG returns the mean, not the total.

explanation: AVG sums the non-NULL values (600) and divides by their count (3), giving 200. To treat NULL as zero you must write AVG(COALESCE(salary, 0)), which would give 150.
concept: Aggregates skip NULL. Use COALESCE if a missing value should count as zero.

body: Which clause must accompany a window function such as ROW_NUMBER()?

options.body: OVER, which defines the partitioning and ordering of the window
GROUP BY
options.whyWrong: Window functions deliberately avoid collapsing rows, which is what GROUP BY does.

options.body: HAVING
options.whyWrong: HAVING filters groups and is unrelated to window definitions.

options.body: DISTINCT
options.whyWrong: DISTINCT deduplicates the result and is not required by window functions.

explanation: Every window function needs an OVER clause. It specifies PARTITION BY (which rows form each window) and ORDER BY (the order within it).
concept: Window function = function + OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...).

body: How do RANK() and DENSE_RANK() differ when there is a tie?

options.body: RANK leaves a gap after the tied rows; DENSE_RANK does not
RANK breaks the tie arbitrarily; DENSE_RANK keeps them tied
options.whyWrong: Both keep tied rows at the same rank.

options.body: DENSE_RANK leaves a gap; RANK does not
options.whyWrong: This reverses the two.

options.body: They are identical except for performance
options.whyWrong: The numbering after a tie genuinely differs.

explanation: With values 90, 90, 80: RANK gives 1, 1, 3 while DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2. ROW_NUMBER would give 1, 2, 3 and break the tie arbitrarily.
concept: RANK skips, DENSE_RANK does not, ROW_NUMBER never ties.

body: Why can a window function not be referenced in the WHERE clause of the same SELECT?

options.body: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, so the value does not exist yet at filter time
Window functions return multiple values per row
options.whyWrong: They return exactly one value per row.

options.body: WHERE only accepts columns, not expressions
options.whyWrong: WHERE accepts arbitrary expressions.

options.body: It is allowed in every major database
options.whyWrong: It is not — the standard evaluation order forbids it.

explanation: Logical evaluation order runs FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, then window functions, then SELECT. To filter on a window result, wrap the query in a subquery or CTE and filter outside it.
concept: To filter a window result, compute it in a CTE and filter in the outer query.

body: What is the difference between a correlated and a non-correlated subquery?

options.body: A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it is conceptually evaluated per outer row
A correlated subquery always returns a single value
options.whyWrong: Correlation concerns the reference to the outer row, not the shape of the result.

options.body: A non-correlated subquery cannot appear in WHERE
options.whyWrong: It appears in WHERE routinely, typically with IN or a comparison.

options.body: A correlated subquery cannot use aggregates
options.whyWrong: Correlated subqueries use aggregates frequently.

explanation: A non-correlated subquery is independent and can be evaluated once. A correlated one depends on the current outer row, so it is logically re-evaluated for each — often the reason such a query is slow.
concept: If the inner query mentions the outer alias, it is correlated.

body: Why can "NOT IN (SELECT col FROM t)" return no rows unexpectedly?

options.body: If the subquery returns any NULL, every NOT IN comparison evaluates to unknown and no rows qualify
NOT IN cannot be used with a subquery
options.whyWrong: It can; the NULL behaviour is the pitfall.

options.body: NOT IN requires the subquery to be sorted
options.whyWrong: No ordering requirement exists.

options.body: NOT IN silently converts to an inner join
options.whyWrong: No such conversion occurs.

explanation: x NOT IN (1, NULL) asks whether x <> 1 AND x <> NULL. The second comparison is unknown, so the whole predicate is never true. Use NOT EXISTS, or filter the NULLs out of the subquery.
concept: A single NULL in a NOT IN list empties the result. Prefer NOT EXISTS.

body: What does EXISTS return compared with IN when the subquery result is large?

options.body: EXISTS can stop at the first matching row, so it often performs better and is NULL-safe
EXISTS materialises the full subquery result first
options.whyWrong: EXISTS is defined to short-circuit on the first match.

options.body: IN is always faster than EXISTS
options.whyWrong: Neither is universally faster; EXISTS avoids the NULL trap and can short-circuit.

options.body: EXISTS requires the subquery to select exactly one column
options.whyWrong: EXISTS ignores the select list entirely.

explanation: EXISTS asks only whether at least one row matches, so it can stop immediately, and it is unaffected by NULLs in the subquery — the two reasons it is usually preferred to NOT IN.
concept: EXISTS: short-circuits and is NULL-safe. IN: convenient for small, NULL-free lists.

body: What does UNION do that UNION ALL does not?

options.body: It removes duplicate rows from the combined result, at the cost of a sort or hash
It combines results from more tables
options.whyWrong: Both combine exactly the queries you write.

options.body: It preserves the order of the inputs
options.whyWrong: Neither guarantees order without an ORDER BY.

options.body: It allows the inputs to have different column counts
options.whyWrong: Both require matching column counts and compatible types.

explanation: UNION deduplicates and therefore must compare every row against the others. UNION ALL just concatenates, so prefer it whenever duplicates are impossible or acceptable.
concept: UNION ALL unless you genuinely need deduplication.

body: Which query finds the second-highest distinct salary reliably, including when there are ties?

options.body: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)
SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1
options.whyWrong: With a tie at the top this returns the highest salary again, not the second distinct one.

options.body: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary <> MAX(salary)
options.whyWrong: An aggregate cannot appear in WHERE; this does not parse.

options.body: SELECT TOP 2 salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC
options.whyWrong: This returns two rows rather than the second distinct value, and has the same tie problem.

explanation: Taking the maximum of everything strictly below the overall maximum gives the second distinct value regardless of how many employees share the top salary. A DENSE_RANK() = 2 filter also works.
concept: "Second distinct" means max of the values below the max — OFFSET counts rows, not distinct values.

body: A CTE is defined with WITH and referenced twice in the main query. What does the standard guarantee about evaluation?

options.body: Nothing about how many times it is evaluated — engines may inline it, so it is not a caching mechanism
It is always evaluated exactly once and the result reused
options.whyWrong: Several engines inline a CTE into each reference, evaluating it more than once.

options.body: It is always evaluated once per reference
options.whyWrong: Some engines do materialise it once; the behaviour is engine-specific.

options.body: It is evaluated lazily and only if a row is requested
options.whyWrong: Lazy evaluation is not a property CTEs guarantee.

explanation: CTEs are primarily a readability construct. Whether one is materialised or inlined varies by engine and version, so never rely on a CTE to memoise an expensive subquery — some engines offer an explicit MATERIALIZED hint for that.
concept: A CTE names a query; it does not promise to compute it only once.

body: Which statement about GROUP BY is correct in standard SQL?

options.body: Every non-aggregated column in the SELECT list must appear in the GROUP BY clause
Any column may appear in SELECT regardless of GROUP BY
options.whyWrong: Some engines permit this in a relaxed mode, but it is not standard and gives an arbitrary value.

options.body: GROUP BY must be accompanied by HAVING
options.whyWrong: HAVING is optional.

options.body: GROUP BY sorts the result by the grouping columns
options.whyWrong: Some engines happen to, but no ordering is guaranteed without ORDER BY.

explanation: The rule exists because a group collapses many rows into one: a column not grouped and not aggregated has no single well-defined value for the group.
concept: Every SELECT column must be grouped or aggregated.

body: What distinguishes method overloading from method overriding?

options.body: Overloading resolves on the signature at compile time; overriding replaces a base implementation and resolves at run time
Overloading happens in subclasses; overriding happens in the same class
options.whyWrong: This reverses the two: overriding is what happens across a class hierarchy.

options.body: Overloading changes the return type only
options.whyWrong: Return type alone is not enough to overload a method in Java or C++.

options.body: Overriding requires a different parameter list
options.whyWrong: A different parameter list makes it an overload, not an override.

explanation: Overloading is several methods with the same name and different parameter lists, chosen by the compiler. Overriding is a subclass replacing an inherited implementation, chosen by the object's actual type at run time.
concept: Overload = compile-time, by signature. Override = run-time, by object type.

body: Why is composition often preferred to inheritance?

options.body: It couples classes only through a narrow interface, and the relationship can change at run time
It always performs better than inheritance
options.whyWrong: Performance is essentially the same; the argument is about coupling.

options.body: Inheritance is deprecated in modern languages

body: What is the time complexity of inserting n elements one by one into a dynamic array that doubles when full?

options.body: O(n) overall, because the amortised cost of each insertion is constant
O(n^2), because each resize copies every element
options.whyWrong: Resizes are geometrically rare, so the copies sum to O(n) rather than O(n^2).

options.body: O(n log n), because there are log n resizes
options.whyWrong: There are log n resizes, but their costs form a geometric series summing to O(n).

options.body: O(log n), because the array doubles
options.whyWrong: Every insertion does at least constant work, so n insertions cannot be sub-linear.

explanation: Doubling means the copies cost 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n, a geometric series bounded by 2n. Spread across n insertions the amortised cost is O(1) each.
concept: Geometric growth makes resizing amortised O(1); growing by a constant would make it O(n^2).

body: A recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). What does it solve to?

options.body: O(n log n)
O(n)
options.whyWrong: The work per level is O(n) and there are log n levels, so the total is not O(n).

options.whyWrong: Each level alone does O(n) work, so the total cannot be logarithmic.

explanation: Each level of recursion does O(n) work across all its subproblems, and there are log n levels. This is the merge sort recurrence.
concept: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) is the merge-sort recurrence: O(n log n).

body: Why is amortised complexity different from average-case complexity?

options.body: Amortised bounds hold for any sequence of operations; average-case bounds assume a distribution over inputs
They are the same thing under different names
options.whyWrong: They rest on quite different assumptions, one worst-case over sequences and one probabilistic.

options.whyWrong: It applies to any sequence of operations on a data structure.

options.body: Average case is always the tighter bound
options.whyWrong: Neither is systematically tighter; they measure different things.

explanation: Amortised analysis is a worst-case guarantee spread over a sequence — no adversarial input can break it. Average-case analysis assumes inputs are drawn from a distribution, which an adversary may violate.
concept: Amortised = worst case over a sequence. Average = expected over a distribution.

body: What is the space complexity of the recursive quicksort in the worst case?

options.body: O(n), because the recursion can degenerate to n nested calls
O(1), because quicksort sorts in place
options.whyWrong: In-place partitioning still leaves the call stack, which is the space being asked about.

options.body: O(n log n), matching its average time
options.whyWrong: Stack depth cannot exceed the number of elements.

options.body: O(log n) in all cases
options.whyWrong: That holds only when partitions are balanced or the recursion on the larger side is eliminated.

explanation: With consistently unbalanced partitions the recursion nests n deep. Recursing on the smaller side and looping on the larger bounds the stack at O(log n).
concept: In-place does not mean O(1) space — count the call stack.

body: Two algorithms are O(n) and O(n log n). For which inputs might the O(n log n) one be faster?

options.body: Small inputs, where the constant factors hidden by the notation dominate
Large inputs, where log n grows slowly
options.whyWrong: Asymptotics favour the O(n) algorithm precisely as n grows.

options.body: Never — big-O ordering holds at every input size
options.whyWrong: Big-O describes growth for sufficiently large n and says nothing about small inputs.

options.body: Only when the input is already sorted
options.whyWrong: Sortedness is a property of specific algorithms, not of the asymptotic comparison.

explanation: Big-O discards constants. An O(n) algorithm with a large constant can lose to an O(n log n) one until n is big enough for the growth rates to dominate — which is why library sorts switch to insertion sort on small subarrays.
concept: Asymptotics describe large n; constants decide small n.

body: What does the two-pointer technique require of the input to work on a "find a pair summing to k" problem?

options.body: The array must be sorted, so a pointer can be moved based on whether the sum is too small or too large
The array must contain only positive numbers
options.whyWrong: The technique works with negatives too, provided the array is sorted.

options.body: The array must have no duplicates
options.whyWrong: Duplicates are handled with a small adjustment and are not a barrier.

options.body: The array must have even length
options.whyWrong: Length parity is irrelevant.

explanation: Sortedness is what makes the pointer movement decidable: too small means advance the left pointer, too large means retreat the right one. On unsorted input a hash set is the usual alternative.
concept: Two pointers need order; a hash set does not.

body: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum subarray sum. What is its core recurrence?

options.body: best_ending_here = max(current element, best_ending_here + current element)
best_ending_here = best_ending_here + current element
options.whyWrong: Without the reset, a long negative prefix drags every later sum down.

options.whyWrong: This omits the extension case and misses sums that build over several elements.

options.whyWrong: A running total is not a maximum-subarray computation.

explanation: At each element you either extend the previous best-ending-here or start fresh from the current element. The overall answer is the maximum of these values.
concept: Extend or restart, and track the best seen so far.

body: Why does a hash table degrade to O(n) lookup in the worst case?

options.body: If every key hashes to the same bucket, the lookup becomes a linear scan of that bucket's chain
Because the table must be resized on every insertion
options.whyWrong: Resizes are geometrically rare and amortise away.

options.body: Because hashing itself is O(n)
options.whyWrong: Hashing a fixed-size key is O(1); the cost is in collisions.

options.whyWrong: Hash tables impose no ordering at all.

explanation: O(1) is an average over a good hash distribution. Adversarial or pathological keys can collide into one bucket, at which point the structure behaves like a list. Some languages randomise the hash seed to prevent deliberate attacks.
concept: Hash tables are O(1) on average and O(n) when everything collides.

body: What is the difference between open addressing and separate chaining?

options.body: Chaining stores colliding entries in a structure per bucket; open addressing probes for another slot in the table itself
Open addressing allows a load factor above 1
options.whyWrong: Open addressing cannot exceed a load factor of 1 — chaining can.

options.body: Chaining requires a perfect hash function
options.whyWrong: Chaining is precisely what tolerates an imperfect hash.

options.body: Open addressing cannot support deletion
options.whyWrong: Deletion is possible with tombstone markers, though it is fiddlier.

explanation: Chaining keeps a list or tree per bucket and tolerates load factors above 1. Open addressing keeps everything in one array, which gives better cache behaviour but degrades sharply as the table fills.
concept: Chaining: flexible, pointer-heavy. Open addressing: cache-friendly, fills badly.

body: What is the time complexity of checking whether two strings of length n are anagrams using a character count?

options.body: O(n), with O(1) extra space for a fixed alphabet
O(n log n), because the strings must be sorted
options.whyWrong: Sorting is one approach, but counting avoids it.

options.body: O(n^2), comparing every character against every other
options.whyWrong: Counting requires only one pass over each string.

options.body: O(1), because only the lengths need comparing
options.whyWrong: Equal lengths do not make two strings anagrams.

explanation: One pass increments a count per character of the first string and decrements for the second; all counts ending at zero means anagram. For a fixed alphabet the count array is constant space.
concept: Counting beats sorting for anagram checks: O(n) instead of O(n log n).

body: Why is repeated string concatenation in a loop often O(n^2) in languages with immutable strings?

options.body: Each concatenation allocates a new string and copies everything accumulated so far
Because string comparison is O(n)
options.whyWrong: No comparison takes place during concatenation.

options.body: Because the garbage collector runs on every iteration
options.whyWrong: Collection timing is not what produces the quadratic behaviour.

options.body: Because strings are stored as linked lists
options.whyWrong: Immutable strings are contiguous, which is exactly why copying costs.

explanation: Copying a prefix of growing length on each of n iterations sums to O(n^2). A StringBuilder, a list joined at the end, or a rope avoids the repeated copying.
concept: Build into a mutable buffer and join once.

body: What is the sliding-window technique best suited to?

options.body: Problems over contiguous subarrays or substrings where the window can be extended and shrunk incrementally
Problems requiring every subset of the input
options.whyWrong: Subsets are not contiguous and the technique does not apply.

options.body: Problems on sorted arrays only
options.whyWrong: Many sliding-window problems run on unsorted input.

options.body: Problems that can be solved greedily in one pass regardless of structure
options.whyWrong: Not every one-pass greedy problem has a window structure.

explanation: A sliding window turns a nested-loop O(n^2) scan into O(n) by maintaining the answer for the current window incrementally as one end advances and the other catches up.
concept: Contiguity plus an incrementally maintainable summary = sliding window.

body: What property makes a binary search tree degenerate to O(n) search?

options.body: Inserting keys in sorted order, which produces a tree shaped like a linked list
Storing duplicate keys
options.whyWrong: Duplicates can be handled without affecting the height.

options.body: Having an even number of nodes
options.whyWrong: Node count parity has no bearing on shape.

options.body: Storing large values in the nodes
options.whyWrong: Payload size does not change the tree structure.

explanation: A BST's performance depends on its height. Sorted insertions place every new key on the same side, giving a height of n. Self-balancing variants such as AVL and red-black trees prevent this.
concept: BST performance is O(height); balancing is what keeps height at log n.

body: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in ascending order?

options.body: In-order

options.whyWrong: Pre-order visits the root before its subtrees, breaking the ordering.

options.whyWrong: Level-order follows the tree's shape rather than its key order.

concept: In-order on a BST = a sorted sequence.

body: What is the height of a complete binary tree with n nodes?

options.body: Approximately log base 2 of n
Approximately n/2
options.whyWrong: That would describe a nearly degenerate tree.

options.body: Approximately the square root of n
options.whyWrong: No standard tree shape gives this height.

concept: Complete tree: n nodes packed into log2 n levels.

body: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on graphs with negative edge weights?

options.body: It finalises a node's distance when first extracted, and a later negative edge could still reduce it
It cannot represent negative numbers
options.whyWrong: Representation is not the issue; the algorithm's greedy invariant is.

options.body: It loops forever on negative edges

options.body: It requires the graph to be undirected
options.whyWrong: Dijkstra works on directed graphs.

explanation: Dijkstra assumes that extending a path never shortens it, which lets it commit to a node's distance permanently. A negative edge breaks that assumption. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights at O(VE).
concept: Dijkstra needs non-negative weights; use Bellman-Ford otherwise.

body: When is BFS preferable to DFS for finding a path between two nodes?

options.body: When the shortest path in number of edges is required on an unweighted graph
When memory is severely constrained
options.whyWrong: BFS holds a whole frontier and generally uses more memory than DFS.

options.body: When the graph is very deep

explanation: BFS explores by distance, so the first time it reaches the target it has used the fewest edges. DFS gives no such guarantee.
concept: Unweighted shortest path = BFS. Weighted = Dijkstra.

body: What does a topological sort require of the graph?

options.body: It must be a directed acyclic graph
It must be connected
options.whyWrong: A DAG with several components still has a valid topological order.

options.body: It must be undirected
options.whyWrong: Edge direction is what defines the ordering.

options.whyWrong: Weights play no part in a topological sort.

explanation: A topological order lists every node before all nodes it points to. A cycle makes that impossible, so the graph must be acyclic and directed. Failure to produce a full order is itself a cycle detector.
concept: Topological sort exists exactly when the directed graph has no cycle.

body: What operation is a min-heap optimised for?

options.body: Retrieving and removing the smallest element, in O(1) and O(log n) respectively
Searching for an arbitrary element
options.whyWrong: Arbitrary search in a heap is O(n); it is not ordered beyond the parent-child relation.

options.body: Finding the largest element
options.whyWrong: That is a max-heap; in a min-heap the largest is somewhere among the leaves.

concept: Heaps give you the extreme cheaply and nothing else.

body: How do you find the k largest elements of n items efficiently when k is much smaller than n?

options.body: Maintain a min-heap of size k, giving O(n log k)

concept: k largest → min-heap of size k. k smallest → max-heap of size k.

body: What two properties must a problem have for dynamic programming to apply?

options.body: Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems

options.body: Overlapping subproblems and a sorted input

body: What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?

options.body: Memoisation is top-down and caches results of recursive calls; tabulation is bottom-up and fills a table iteratively

options.whyWrong: Both usually store the same number of states; the difference is direction, not asymptotic cost.

concept: Top-down caches what it visits; bottom-up computes everything but avoids the stack.

body: What makes a greedy algorithm provably correct for a problem?

options.body: The greedy choice property — a locally optimal choice is part of some globally optimal solution

options.whyWrong: Speed says nothing about correctness.

options.body: That the input is sorted before processing

body: Which sorting algorithm is stable and guarantees O(n log n) in the worst case?

options.body: Heap sort

options.body: Selection sort

concept: Merge: stable, O(n log n) guaranteed, O(n) space. Heap: O(n log n) guaranteed, in place, unstable.

body: Why does binary search require random access rather than merely a sorted sequence?

options.whyWrong: Any totally ordered type works.

options.whyWrong: No such restriction exists.

body: What is the standard way to detect a cycle in a singly linked list in O(1) space?

options.body: Count the nodes and compare with the known length

body: Why is a stack the natural structure for checking balanced brackets?

options.body: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed, which is exactly last-in-first-out order
Because brackets must be counted
options.whyWrong: Counting alone cannot distinguish "([)]" from "([])".

options.body: Because a stack sorts its contents
options.whyWrong: Stacks impose no ordering on values.

options.body: Because the input is read backwards
options.whyWrong: The check runs left to right.

concept: Any nesting problem is a stack problem.

body: What is the base case failure that causes a stack overflow in a recursive function?

options.body: The recursion never reaches a condition that returns without recursing further
The function allocates too much heap memory
options.whyWrong: Heap exhaustion produces an out-of-memory error, not a stack overflow.

options.body: The function has too many parameters
options.whyWrong: Parameter count affects frame size marginally, not termination.

options.body: The function returns the wrong value
options.whyWrong: A wrong value is a logic bug, not an overflow.

explanation: Every recursion needs a base case that the recursive calls provably approach. If the argument does not shrink toward it, the call stack grows without bound.

body: What are the four Coffman conditions that must all hold for a deadlock?

options.body: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait
Mutual exclusion, starvation, priority inversion, and circular wait
options.whyWrong: Starvation and priority inversion are separate problems, not deadlock conditions.

options.body: Hold and wait, preemption, aging, and circular wait
options.whyWrong: Preemption and aging prevent deadlock rather than causing it.

options.body: Race conditions, mutual exclusion, context switching, and no preemption
options.whyWrong: Race conditions and context switching are not among the conditions.

body: What is the difference between deadlock and starvation?

options.body: In deadlock no process in the set can ever proceed; in starvation a process could proceed but is perpetually passed over
They are the same condition under different names
options.whyWrong: The distinction is whether progress is impossible or merely never granted.

options.body: Deadlock affects threads and starvation affects processes
options.whyWrong: Both affect either.

options.body: Starvation always leads to deadlock
options.whyWrong: Starvation can persist indefinitely without any deadlock.

concept: Deadlock: nobody can move. Starvation: somebody could, but never gets the chance.

body: Why is a mutex not interchangeable with a semaphore initialised to 1?

options.whyWrong: A binary semaphore can provide mutual exclusion, which is why the two are often confused.

options.body: A mutex allows several threads into the critical section
options.whyWrong: A mutex admits exactly one.

options.body: A semaphore is always faster
options.whyWrong: Relative speed depends on the implementation, not on the abstraction.

concept: Mutex = ownership and mutual exclusion. Semaphore = a counter for signalling.

body: What problem does a condition variable solve that a mutex alone does not?

options.body: Waiting for a state change without holding the lock or spinning, and being woken when it occurs

options.whyWrong: That is exactly what the mutex does.

options.body: Preventing deadlock automatically

options.body: Making critical sections faster
options.whyWrong: Speed is not what they address.

body: What is thrashing in a virtual memory system?

options.body: The system spends most of its time paging because the active working set exceeds physical memory

options.whyWrong: Excessive context switching is a different overhead problem.

options.body: The disk fragments over time
options.whyWrong: Fragmentation is a file-system concern.

options.body: Cache lines are evicted by competing threads
options.whyWrong: That is cache thrashing, at a different level of the hierarchy.

explanation: When the combined working sets do not fit in RAM, every process faults on pages just evicted from another. Throughput collapses; the fix is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming or add memory.

body: What is the key difference between paging and segmentation?

options.body: Paging divides memory into fixed-size blocks; segmentation divides it into variable-size logical units

options.whyWrong: Both are hardware-supported on architectures that provide them.

options.body: Paging causes external fragmentation
options.whyWrong: Fixed-size pages eliminate external fragmentation; segmentation is what suffers from it.

options.body: Segmentation requires no address translation
options.whyWrong: Segmentation translates addresses through a segment table.

explanation: Fixed-size pages eliminate external fragmentation at the cost of some internal waste. Variable-size segments match program structure but leave unusable gaps as segments are loaded and removed.
concept: Paging: internal fragmentation. Segmentation: external fragmentation.

body: Why can a process have many threads sharing one address space but not one file descriptor per thread by default?

options.whyWrong: Cost is not the reason; sharing is the defining property of threads.

options.body: Threads cannot perform I/O
options.whyWrong: Threads perform I/O routinely.

options.body: The kernel does not track threads individually
options.whyWrong: The kernel schedules threads individually; it is the resources that are shared.

explanation: A thread is a schedulable execution context within a process. Sharing the address space and descriptor table is what distinguishes threads from processes — and is why thread bugs corrupt shared state so readily.
concept: Threads share everything but their stack and registers.
